new_statements.citation: Zemp, Marius. 2018. A Grammar of Purik Tibetan (Brill's Tibetan Studies Library 21). Leiden: Brill. DOI 10.1163/9789004366312.
new_statements.locator: §2.1.4 'Stress', p. 39 (ch. 2 Phonology, pp. 29-101); second sentence p. 44 (Google Books pg=PA39, pg=PA44)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word accent in nouns and other non-verbs falls on the second syllable (and on the fourth in four-syllable words), realised by higher pitch: LH, LHL, LHLH. Verbs (and some morphologically motivated formations) have a first-syllable HLL pattern instead, and negated disyllabic verbal complexes are LH. Accent is weak and mostly non-contrastive; it matters chiefly where it alone separates -pa infinitives from nouns. Zemp treats it as a pitch-realised 'word-accent'/'stress', so 'pitch-accent' is a defensible alternative reading.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 47 snippet: '(... secondary stress on the second syllable), which is, however, strongly subject to variation'; p. 106: 'lexical stress will generally not be indicated' in the grammar's transcriptions except fourth-syllable stress on quadrisyllabics.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs default to HLL (first-syllable accent); LHL vs HLL/LLH accents on trisyllabics are morphologically motivated (e.g. to keep a first syllable from being read as negating ma-); loans acquire the default LH pattern; a few Balti polysyllables with first-syllable stress noted for comparison (Sprigg 1966).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, judged 'in isolation' (citation forms); the grammar also has a separate Prosody chapter (pp. 870-915) on phrase/sentence intonation that was not accessible. Describes the Purik dialect of Kargil only.
new_statements.identity_note: Zemp's grammar describes Purik proper, the Tibetan dialect of Kargil (Ladakh, India), which Glottolog folds into puri1258 'Purik-Sham-Nubra' together with Sham (Lower Ladakhi) and Nubra; no Sham or Nubra stress description was examined. Rangan 1979 and Sharma 2004 also describe Kargil Purki. Balti (balt1258) is a different language, mentioned only comparatively.

sources.note: §2.1.4 'Stress' (p. 39): bi-, tri- and quadrisyllabic non-verbs carry a default word-accent realised as a higher-pitched second (and fourth) syllable (LH / LHL / LHLH); verbs default to HLL (first-syllable accent); p. 44: accent 'does not appear to be a salient feature of Purik' except where it alone distinguishes verbal forms (-pa infinitives) from nouns; p. 47 mentions secondary stress on the second syllable subject to variation; p. 106: lexical stress generally not marked. Brill full text is paywalled (Unpaywall: closed; brill.com returns 403/405 to fetchers); only Google Books search snip…

sources.citation: Bailey, T. Grahame. 1920. Linguistic Studies from the Himalayas: being studies in the grammar of fifteen Himalayan dialects (Asiatic Society Monographs 18). London: Royal Asiatic Society. Purik section.
